I’ve been having a really hard time focusing, especially at work. I’m a mechanical engineer, so I’m usually juggling drawings, emails, calculations. Lately—maybe the past several months—I’ll reread the same line three or four times and still not take it in. I misplace tools or my notebook, leave half-finished tasks open on my screen, and then completely forget to go back to them. My wife says I drift off in the middle of conversations and seem “somewhere else.”

I also keep getting this jolt when someone comes up behind me or a door opens quickly. Even if it’s just a coworker tapping me on the shoulder, my whole body jumps and my heart starts racing. I hate walking through certain parts of the plant because something about the noise and the layout makes me feel on edge and uneasy, like I want to get out of there right away.

I can’t shake this feeling that what happened a while back was somehow my fault, that I should’ve done more or noticed something sooner. I go over it in my head and just feel guilty. Since then, my drive has really dropped off—I have to push myself to start things, and even simple tasks feel like a slog.
D018-D002_h001.question_a:
It started about a year and a half ago, after the accident at the plant. Since then, I just haven’t been the same. Before that, I was pretty sharp at work—design reviews, calculations, keeping track of a dozen things at once were never an issue. But after the accident, my mind feels foggy. I misplace tools and drawings constantly, forget what I was about to do midway through a task, and my wife has to remind me about simple things I never used to miss. This only began after the accident, not when I was a kid or anything.

What really bothers me is how on edge I am. If someone comes up behind me at the shop floor or moves quickly into my field of vision, I practically jump out of my skin. Loud clanks or sudden movement make me brace like something bad is about to happen.

I also can’t shake this feeling that it’s my fault—that I should’ve double-checked the safety protocols, that if I’d noticed one more detail, nobody would’ve been hurt. I go over it in my head constantly, feeling guilty, like I failed them, and it’s drained any drive I had. Even simple projects feel pointless, and I struggle to even get started.
D018-D002_h001.question_b:
Honestly, this has been going on as long as I can remember, way before anything bad happened. Even in elementary school I just couldn’t stay on track. Teachers always said I was “bright but careless” because I’d zone out, miss instructions, lose my homework. It’s the same now at 42. At work, I’ll read a spec three times and still drift off, or start a design and then realize I’ve forgotten a key detail. I misplace tools, forget where I set my phone or keys multiple times a day. My wife jokes about it, but it bothers me—it feels like my brain keeps slipping away.

The accident two years ago made everything heavier emotionally, but the focus issues were already there long before that. Since the accident, whenever I hear screeching tires or see footage of crashes, I get this tight, panicky feeling and can’t think straight. I jump if someone comes around a corner too fast in the shop. I keep replaying it, thinking I should have done something differently, blaming myself, feeling guilty. That guilt just sits there, and it makes it even harder to get started on tasks or finish things I’m supposed to do.

I’ve been out in the woods most of my life, so I’m used to being alone, but the past few years something’s been…off. My mind just doesn’t stay where I put it. I’ll start filling out patrol reports and stare at the page, lose the thread mid-sentence, or forget what I was heading back to the truck for. It’s not just at work—simple things like choosing what to make for dinner or what jacket to wear can have me standing there stuck, going back and forth over nothing.

Every now and then, especially when I’m on a fire line or hear a branch crack behind me, it feels like I’m back in that big fire where my partner died. For a few seconds I’m not in the present; I can smell the smoke, feel the heat, like it’s happening again. If someone comes up behind me and taps my shoulder, I jump out of my skin.

Since that fire, I can’t shake this feeling that I should’ve done something different—that it was my fault somehow. When I get a commendation, or someone praises my work, it just feels empty. I don’t really care about the awards anymore; mostly I just feel this steady guilt sitting in my gut.
D018-D002_h002.question_a:
It started about three years ago, after that big wildfire where two of my crew died. Since then, it’s like part of me is still up on that ridge.

Every so often, especially when I smell smoke or hear a loud crack in the woods, I’m not really in the present anymore. It’s like I’m back there—my heart pounds, I can see their faces, I hear the radio going dead. For a few seconds I honestly forget I’m just walking a trail; I feel like it’s happening all over again.

I jump out of my skin if someone taps me on the shoulder, even my grandson. Any sudden touch from behind and I whip around like I’m under attack. And I can’t seem to make up my mind about anything now—what to wear, what to cook, even which trail to patrol. I’ll stand there frozen, second-guessing myself.

I used to be sharp and organized, ran crews for decades, but my focus went downhill only after that fire. I lose track of what I’m doing mid-task. I keep thinking it’s my fault they died, that I should’ve called the evacuation sooner. I go over it every night, feeling guilty, and honestly, nothing I’ve done since seems to matter much to me anymore.
D018-D002_h002.question_b:
I’ve always had trouble paying attention, even as a kid. My teachers used to say I was “off in the clouds.” I’d be staring out the window instead of listening, and I’d forget homework or lose things. That never really went away. Even now, out on patrol, I’ll drift off in my head and realize I’ve missed radio calls or walked past markers I was supposed to check. Reading reports is hard—I reread the same paragraph over and over and still can’t recall what it said. Making simple decisions, like which route to take first or even what to eat, can take me an embarrassingly long time.

The trauma from my wife’s accident came much later. Since then, I sometimes feel like I’m back at the scene when I hear certain sounds—like the crack of a branch can suddenly feel like metal crunching. If someone taps me on the shoulder unexpectedly, I jump hard. I keep thinking I should’ve been there, that I could’ve stopped it, and I can’t shake this guilt. When people praise my work, it doesn’t mean much; I just feel like I failed at what mattered.

I run a small bakery, so my days start around three in the morning. Lately—maybe the past several months, maybe longer, it all blurs—I keep losing track of things. I’ll put the sugar down and a minute later I’m wandering around the kitchen, no idea where I left it. Sometimes in the middle of taking an order my mind just… drifts, and I have to ask the customer to repeat everything.

What really scares me are these moments where I’m not fully in the room. A certain smell, or a sound, and suddenly it feels like I’m somewhere else entirely, like an old scene is happening again right in front of me. It doesn’t last long, but while it’s happening I’m not in the bakery anymore. If someone taps me on the shoulder during those times, I jump out of my skin. Even a gentle touch from behind, I spin around like I’m being attacked.

I’ve also noticed I don’t really care about the bakery’s success the way I used to. People congratulate me, and I just feel… flat. And when I think about how things went so wrong back then, I still find myself furious at certain people, convinced it’s their fault, and that anger just sits there, simmering all the time.
D018-D002_h003.question_a:
It really started after my husband died in that car accident three years ago. Before that, I could run the bakery, handle orders, bills, everything. Since then, my head just doesn’t work the same. I’ll put the measuring spoons down and five minutes later I’m tearing the place apart because I can’t remember where I left them. I lose track of recipes I’ve made for 30 years. This wasn’t a problem when I was younger; it only began after the crash.

Sometimes, especially when I hear tires screech outside or a tray drops, I’m not in the bakery anymore. I’m right back on that street, seeing his body, smelling the gasoline. It’s like I’m there again, not just remembering it. If someone comes up behind me and taps my shoulder, I jump out of my skin, almost drop the bread.

I used to be proud of building this shop, but now I just feel numb about it, like it doesn’t matter. Underneath, I’m constantly angry—at the driver who hit him, at the hospital, at everyone who “let it happen.” It feels like this low boil that never really shuts off.
D018-D002_h003.question_b:
It’s hard to explain, but I’ve always been “scattered,” even as a kid. Teachers used to say I was smart but “off in my own world,” losing assignments, forgetting instructions. That same thing has followed me my whole life. At the bakery, I’ll start weighing flour, then get distracted by the phone, and when I come back I can’t remember where I left off. I put my keys down and five minutes later I’m wandering around the shop looking for them. It’s gotten worse with age, so I worry it’s my memory, but it feels more like my mind just slips away.

About eight years ago my husband died suddenly in a car accident. Since then, certain things set me off. If someone taps me on the shoulder from behind, I jump out of my skin. Sometimes when I hear tires screech outside, for a moment I feel like I’m right back at the hospital getting the news. I carry a lot of anger about it, and I catch myself blaming the other driver, even fate.
